newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Hong Kong to introduce post-handover sedition laws.
newsitem.headline: Hong Kong to introduce post-handover sedition laws.

text.p: Hong Kong's government said on Tuesday it would introduce changes to an existing law on sedition and treason to protect citizens before and after the territory's handover to China in 1997.
Under present Hong Kong laws, sedition and treason are not offences. But after next year's handover they will be outlawed, as set down in the territory's post-1997 constitution, the Basic Law.
The proposed changes, which the government would attempt to introduce before the June 30 handover, would provide definitions of treason, secession, sedition and subversion.

"It is quite clear that it is the view of the community that we should seek to have legislation on these concepts in place before July 1, 1997," Secretary for Security Peter Lai told a news conference.
The post-1997 constitution has stipulated that the future Hong Kong government will enact laws to ban seditious activities in the territory.
Jittery Hong Kong citizens have been concerned that the post-colonial government will introduce a mainland Chinese interpretation of sedition and treason to snuff out criticism of Chinese policies.
The proposed changes look set to anger Beijing as China has said it deems the changes unnecessary and has refused to discuss the matter with the British colonial government.

"They are not prepared to talk to us about the Basic Law Article 23 relating to treason, subversion, sedition and succession," Lai said. "As a result, we have no alternative but to introduce the bill to the Legislative Council."

The proposed amendment will be published by the government on Friday and introduced to the Legislative Council for a first and second reading on December 4. More than 150 years of colonial rule will end at midnight on June 30 next year when Hong Kong reverts to China as a Special Administrative Region (SAR).
China has promised not to change Hong Kong's capitalist way of life and to allow the territory to enjoy a high degree of autonomy for 50 years after the handover.
